analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans new oil and gas leasing off California's coast.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 28 House members, never received a hearing or vote and died in committee when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written a permanent ban into federal law against new oil and gas leasing on the outer Continental Shelf off California's coast, overriding any future administration's plan to sell drilling rights there. It would not have touched drilling rights already granted before enactment. It was introduced in April 2009, referred to committee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: California's coastal communities — including fishing, tourism, and beach-dependent businesses — and the general public, who would face a lower risk of new offshore drilling platforms, spills, and industrialization of the California coastline. The ban would be permanent and written into statute, so it could not be reversed by a future administration's leasing plan.

how_it_helps.text: Permanently prohibits oil and gas preleasing, leasing, and related activities in all federal waters off the California coast, amending the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act.

The ban is written as a statutory prohibition that applies 'notwithstanding any other provision of this Act or any other law,' meaning no future administration could open California's coast to new drilling through a routine leasing plan.
It was introduced by a California member, Rep. Lois Capps, with 28 cosponsors from the California delegation, giving the state's coastline a unified voice in the bill.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies that could otherwise have bid on new offshore leases off California. Any effect on consumers at the pump would be marginal, since the bill covers only one state's federal waters and would have taken years to produce oil anyway. Coastal residents near existing platforms would bear no new benefit, because the bill leaves all pre-existing leases in place.

drawbacks.text: The ban is only partial: it expressly preserves all rights under leases issued before enactment, so existing drilling platforms off California — and the spill risks that come with them — could continue operating indefinitely.

By foreclosing new leasing, the bill removes one potential source of domestic oil supply, which oil producers argue slightly increases reliance on foreign imports; the practical effect on prices for one state's offshore area would be small.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — a permanent, hard-to-reverse shield over California's federal waters against new drilling — is large for the coastline's environment, fisheries, and tourism economy, and the cost is limited to foregone drilling opportunities for one industry in one region. The main weakness is that the bill leaves existing leases untouched, so the risk it addresses is reduced, not eliminated.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to its Energy and Mineral Resources subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Lois Capps introduced the bill on April 2, 2009 with 28 original cosponsors, all Democrats from California.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources; on April 13, 2009 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources.
No further action was ever taken — the bill never received a hearing or vote in the subcommittee, the full committee, or the House, and it expired when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and gas interests are better off: no statutory ban now stands in the way of future leasing decisions off California, and the bill's failure left existing leases fully intact.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Offshore oil interests and existing leaseholders

for.name: Lois Capps
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 28 cosponsors, all from the California delegation.

against.name: Nick Rahall
against.what_they_did: The committee received the bill and never scheduled a markup or vote; it stalled at the subcommittee level until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call exists; all 28 cosponsors were Democrats, but the committee that buried it was also run by Democrats.

industries.note: The bill would have permanently closed federal waters off California to new oil and gas leasing, eliminating future bidding opportunities for drilling companies. Its interest in keeping those waters open runs against the coastal protection the public gets from the ban.

industries.industry: Existing California leaseholders and platform operators
industries.note: The bill explicitly preserves all rights under leases issued before its enactment, so companies already drilling off California keep operating with no new restrictions. That grandfather clause means the risk from current platforms continues even as new competition is barred.
Blocking new drilling protects beaches, fisheries, and coastal views that the tourism and fishing economies depend on. A single major spill off California would hit these industries directly.
